clinicalPearls: Mitochondrial disorder usually caused by a single large-scale deletion of mitochondrial DNA, typically sporadic
Defined by a classic triad: onset before the age of twenty, progressive external ophthalmoplegia and pigmentary retinopathy
At least one of cardiac conduction block, cerebrospinal fluid protein above one gram per litre, or cerebellar ataxia is required to complete the diagnosis
The pigmentary retinopathy has a salt-and-pepper appearance and may cause relatively mild visual symptoms
Progressive cardiac conduction disease can culminate in complete heart block and sudden death, warranting close cardiac monitoring and timely pacing
Additional features include proximal myopathy, sensorineural deafness, short stature and endocrinopathies such as diabetes and hypoparathyroidism
Muscle biopsy classically shows ragged-red fibres and cytochrome c oxidase-deficient fibres
Elevated blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and molecular analysis of mitochondrial DNA support the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Kearns-Sayre syndrome usually results from a single large-scale deletion of mitochondrial DNA arising during oogenesis or early embryogenesis, so it is generally sporadic. The deletion removes genes encoding subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation chain and mitochondrial transfer RNAs, impairing energy production. Heteroplasmic distribution of deleted genomes across tissues, with a bias toward post-mitotic high-energy-demand organs such as extraocular muscle, retina, cardiac conduction tissue, brain and endocrine glands, explains the characteristic multisystem phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia without the full syndrome
Other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies such as MELAS and MERRF
Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome (which can evolve into Kearns-Sayre syndrome)
Congenital or acquired causes of pigmentary retinopathy
additionalInvestigations: ECG and Holter monitoring for conduction disease, with cardiology surveillance
Molecular analysis for a single large-scale mitochondrial DNA deletion
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and cerebrospinal fluid protein
Muscle biopsy for ragged-red and cytochrome c oxidase-deficient fibres
Endocrine screen and audiometry for associated organ involvement
redFlags: New or progressive cardiac conduction block, syncope or bradyarrhythmia
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive and multisystem; prognosis is largely determined by cardiac conduction disease, which can cause sudden death and is mitigated by surveillance and pacing. Life expectancy is reduced, with care focused on supportive and organ-specific management.
pitfalls: Failing to institute cardiac surveillance and offer timely pacing for conduction block
Mistaking the ophthalmoplegia for myasthenia gravis
Not recognising that Pearson syndrome in a survivor may evolve into Kearns-Sayre syndrome
management: Cardiac conduction surveillance with regular ECG and Holter monitoring and timely pacemaker insertion for progressive block, since conduction disease drives mortality
Consideration of a defibrillator-capable device given the risk of sudden death from complete heart block
Supportive mitochondrial cofactor supplementation such as coenzyme Q10, with avoidance of mitochondrial-toxic drugs including sodium valproate and aminoglycosides
Ophthalmological management of ptosis and ophthalmoplegia with ptosis props or surgery, and low-vision support for the pigmentary retinopathy
Endocrine screening and replacement for associated diabetes, hypoparathyroidism and other endocrinopathies
Audiological rehabilitation with hearing aids or cochlear implantation for sensorineural deafness, plus physiotherapy and swallowing support for proximal myopathy
Clinical genetics and metabolic specialist input with counselling; recurrence risk is usually low as single large-scale deletions are typically sporadic
